---
title: "Sliding Window: Only Two Items Change"
description: "A mathematical technique worth memorising for algorithm interviews."
---

## Recognition trigger

Fixed-length consecutive sums, rolling counts and neighbouring windows.

## Problem to think through

**Why is it wasteful to recompute a whole window when it moves one position?**

## Formula worth memorising

$$
W_{i+1}=W_i-a_i+a_{i+k}
$$

**Every symbol explained:** W_i is the sum of the k elements beginning at index i; a_i is the outgoing leftmost element; a_{i+k} is the incoming new element; k is fixed window length.

**Substitute actual values:** With a=[2,4,1,5], k=3, first sum W0=2+4+1=7. Shift right: W1=7−2+5=10. We didn't rescan the shared middle elements 4 and 1.

## Why the derivation is valid

The old and new fixed-size windows share exactly k−1 elements. All common terms cancel, leaving only one subtraction and addition per shift, so all n−k+1 windows take O(n) total time.

## What could invalidate it?

The formula is for additive fixed-size windows. A maximum/minimum requires different state, often a monotonic deque; variable-length windows require a valid invariant.

## The 20-second memory card

**Memorise: Adjacent windows overlap: subtract the one leaving, add the one entering.**

Reconstruct the proof from the example rather than memorising the code.

**Interview problems:** Maximum Average Subarray; Maximum Sum of Size K.

**Research reference:** [Read the mathematical method](https://usaco.guide/gold/sliding-window). The worked numbers and explanation are independently written.
